utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Any matters to mention at this stage? Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just a very brief matter, Your Honour. The next witness was -- we were scheduled to bring him in sometime around 4.00 or so; however, since we will not be reaching that witness - he's requesting protective measures, so I'd rather not say his name - I'd ask that he be released for the day and be brought in tomorrow. I've discussed it with counsel, and there doesn't seem to be any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, your request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: While the being is secured, could I just indicate that I'm going to continue questioning him on Defence document D66, that was the document yesterday. MFI221, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So that we could have that document on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. Yesterday I was asking you some questions about a particular document of Namik Dzankovic, and I just have some final questions about that document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the court staff please assist me for a moment by providing a -- a paper copy of this document to Mr. Jasarevic, which he was looking at yesterday. Your Honours, the reason for providing the paper copy is that on the screen the B/C/S version is marred by some -- some highlight or pen markings, and so that's why he's being given it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, yesterday I was -- I'd asked you a number of questions about this document. And you indicated to me that you viewed that some of the -- some of the proposals by Mr. Dzankovic appeared somewhat unrealistic. I just want to ask you about the details of that with respect to some of the specific proposals. Would you look towards the end of the document, please, at those specific proposals of -- of Mr. Dzankovic. And I'll take you one by one to them and get your comments about them. Do you see -- do you have in front of you those proposals?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have in front of you the suggestion by Mr. Dzankovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is on page 3 of the English version, and it's -- it's essentially the last -- the last four paragraphs of the -- on the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. Now, you'll see there that there are a number of proposals. I just want you to comment on the first one. The first proposal seems to be a proposal to -- and I quote: "Continue gathering operative information." Now, could I just ask you: Was that a appropriate proposal for Mr. Dzankovic to -- to pursue?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I provided a lot of comments regarding operative information, operative work. This proposal definitely makes sense. But as I said yesterday, one thing I failed to understand is why he's putting this forward as a proposal and who the proposal is addressed to, to himself or to someone else. It certainly does make sense, however, to gather operative information at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. And just to pursue a comment that you made both now and yesterday. You personally were in no position sitting in your office in Sarajevo and burdened with the tasks that you had to do to perform any of these tasks listed here; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely. It wasn't my understanding at the time that he was bringing these proposals to me or to my administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, I understand that. Does it -- but just relying on your own experience here of -- and -- and also your knowledge of -- of the concrete case, does it appear to you that what you had here was Mr. Dzankovic in an unfamiliar situation turning to a senior person for perhaps advice, guidance, and comfort? Is that how it reads to you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are elements in this document to suggest that kind of interpretation; however, I believe there's something else missing here, Your Honours. When I look at these proposals by Mr. Dzankovic, it's very difficult for me to understand his position, his ideas, or what he wants to achieve. This, of course, follows from the task that he had been given by Mr. Sefer Halilovic. I must expand on this, Your Honours, taking one thing at a time. If Dzankovic is a member of the inspection team, if Mr. Halilovic is the leader of the inspection team, there's one thing I don't understand, and this is what I had in mind when I spoke about these assignments given to Mr. Dzankovic not being realistic. I don't see a commanding authority here, someone who would have issued an order to carry out an assignment as complex as this, an assignment that would have entailed an on-site investigation. This assignment, which in my opinion was given to Dzankovic by Mr. Halilovic, does make sense. What I recognise when I look at it is that Mr. Halilovic was surprised and that he certainly wanted something done in this respect. However, there are a number of other significant details that one needs to bear in mind. In every report, you find warnings about the dangers entailed in moving about the area. It is quite obvious that conditions are imposed by Mr. Delalic in relation to removing the units that were there, which also relates to their combat tasks being carried out. And now I'm inching closer to my own explanation. Why did I say that these assignments were unrealistic? One thing, Your Honours, that I can't figure out is how these were to be implemented, the tasks that Dzankovic extrapolated from the assignment given him by Mr. Halilovic. I see no realistic possibility for Mr. Dzankovic to be able to do anything about this without enlisting the assistance of some forces on the ground. It was down to them to carry this out. Rather strong forces, in fact, a battalion or two of the military police, for instance. How, without enlisting the assistance of the Ministry of the Interior's police officers? How without clear orders from the operation commander? Someone in a position of authority, someone to issue orders to the right people in the right places. I mean, the professional people supposed to carry out an on-site investigation as well as the units themselves. This sort of approach to the assignment would only have been realistic under these conditions. So as I said back at the outset, these tasks do make sense. The problem is they are simply not realistic. Later on you will see what our reaction was back in the administration when we realised about this document. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May I just intervene for one moment there. I have the intention of taking you to some of those documents which indicate your reaction, and you will certainly be asked those questions. There's just a translation issue that's arisen here which I want to clarify, and, Mr. Jasarevic, at page --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at page 5, line 1 the translation has -- reads as follows: "What I recognise when I look at it is that Mr. Halilovic was not surprised and that he certainly wanted something done in this respect." Now, I'm instructed that the witness said that he was surprised, that Mr. Halilovic was surprised, and that he wanted something done in that respect. And could I just ask, first of all, whether the interpreter would be prepared to clarify what the situation was with that answer, and then I'll -- I'll ask the witness also to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think you better ask the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. This is entirely outside your control. There was a translation of your words before in the way that I just -- that you heard me say. Was it your evidence that it appears that Mr. Halilovic was surprised or was not surprised?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this may be about words. I believe I understand the situation, and again I'm trying to interpret these two words said by Dzankovic under quotation marks, saying -- distancing himself or dissociating himself from the crime. My reading of this is very unequivocal. Mr. Halilovic is against the crime. I'm not sure if I'm making myself any clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, that -- you've made it clear that that's what your answer is, and those are the only questions I have about it. Could I just pursue a couple of specific questions about a couple of the proposals made. I hear what you say about the -- the first proposal -- or sorry, the second of the proposals. Could I ask you to just comment on the appropriateness of interviewing members of Adnan Solakovic's unit. Did that appear to be a sensible and appropriate measure for Dzankovic to suggest? And, of course, I understand the -- the issues that you've raised in other respects, but just in terms of that as an appropriate measure, an appropriate investigative measure, did that seem to make sense to you, to take statements from Solakovic's men?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proposal was inappropriate in terms of timing. I provided a lengthy explanation of my own position a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I believe that explanation also answered at least part of your present question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, I follow that. Could you go to the next paragraph there, and notice that one of Dzankovic's suggestions was to request a report from Zulfikar Alispago. Now, could I just ask you first of all: Did they ever show you any such report from Zulfikar Alispago?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. If you want me to comment on his proposal, his request, I believe we had another proposal where he says, Give an order to set up a mixed commission, including members of the MUP and of the SVB, and so on and so forth. Again, I will give you my position on this. He's requesting a report from the unit commanders, Zulfikar and so on and so forth. Here again I must say I don't understand Dzankovic's view on this situation, being a member of the inspection team as he was. These are assignments that should stem from a different level. There should be an order, as they say in assignment number 2. Who on earth could have requested Zulfikar to draft a report? I believe the most appropriate term to use in this context is the one I have already used, "unrealistic." You can see that people are striving for something here, that there are certain aspirations and ambitions, a desire to achieve something, but this still stops far short from actually managing to do a decent job. And I'm talking about the on-site investigation that needs to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And just -- sorry, just to conclude that matter, you've given us a -- a theoretical and a very useful theoretical explanation there, if I may say so. May I just ask whether or not the report -- do you see there that there's a reference made to a report by Zulfikar Alispago which is, according to this note, already written? Do you see that, that passage there, where it says "request a report from Zulfikar Alispago who, as he says himself, wrote a report and forwarded it to the Sarajevo SVK." Now, my question about that really is this: As Dzankovic referred to this particular report of Zulfikar Alispago, which was already supposed to be written, do you recall whether you received or even heard of the SVK receiving such a report, or at the time did you receive no such news at all?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I received no such news at all. I don't remember having heard anything about it, and I've certainly never seen a report like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, the next document I would ask that the witness be shown is D149. That is -- sorry, now, that's the 65 ter number. So just before that's -- that's sought, I'll provide the double-D number. It's DD00.0662, and it's to be MFI222.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, while that document is being produced, can I indicate what it is that's coming. It's the report of Mr. Salihamidzic, which I think you gave evidence was suggested -- was annexed to the Dzankovic report. Do you have that in front of you on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the print is very small, and I can hardly distinguish anything. But what you said is quite right. I remember the note by Mr. Salihamidzic quite clearly. He was the deputy chief of the Jablanica public security station. I have it here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask you about -- Mr. Jasarevic, it's -- there's no purpose in my reading this document onto the transcript. I'm proposing to tender it -- offer it for tender as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just indicate this, that Mr. Salihamidzic will be giving evidence in the Prosecution case course and, in any event, it would go through him, but I'll be tendering it now, if permitted to do so, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And although I'm not going to read it out to you and get you to agree with every line in it or to comment on every line in it, there are a couple of matter in there that I want you to comment about. The first one is this: There is a paragraph or a section that begins with the words: "On the 10th of September, 1993, I interviewed Ivan Pranjic." It's on the first page, and it may be at the start of the last big paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Excellent. Very well, then --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the English version, it's on page 2, and it's perhaps six or seven lines from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I just wanted to ask you about this: When a policeman says in a statement that they have interviewed a person, according to the practice at the time does that mean that a written statement would have been obtained?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Especially as concerns members of the public security station. I don't know these people involved personally, but I do assume that there were better-trained officers around to do this sort of work. In order to interview a crucial witness, I dare say, in a matter like this -- or rather, having the possibility to take a statement from this witness, it is clear that there is good information here, which is not usually the case in this matter. Sometimes you only find someone's first name and sometimes only their last name, whereas here you have more information on these persons. And in my opinion, this shouldn't be -- this should have been written up as a formal statement. And not only this person's statement but, rather, all the other 14 people who'd been evacuated. They should have struck, as we say, while the iron was still hot. We all know from our professional experience that as time goes by, it's very difficult to get good and reliable operative information at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, and thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just would you excuse me for one moment. Your Honours, I'm sorry, I'm just advised now that in terms of the English translation, there may be a catch. And I just want to make sure that everyone is able to look at the right document here. There are in the English translation -- could I just ask perhaps before I go into that: Do Your Honours have the right page in front of you now? Am I able to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean by "the right page"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, what's on our screen now is -- and this is -- this is not the fault of anyone in court. It's -- it's just a labeling sort of issue. There are two documents together here, two Defence documents together, so that what needs to be shown in the English version is really page 4 and not page 2. There's -- it's a scanning issue. But if you look to page 4, you'll be able to see the -- the proper version. And it's about six lines from the top. So I apologise for that. It's page 2 of this document, but this document is only one part of what's been scanned in, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, sorry, I won't ask you about the -- the substance of that -- of this document. And I'm really asking about the taking of statements. Would you mind now moving to another interview, which this witness talks about. You may see a -- a section beginning with the words "Together with Semsudin Halebic [phoen], a security officer of the Jablanica OPS, I interviewed Alija Turkic." Does that passage appear on the page that you have?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If so, it would be down -- very much down the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semsudin Halebic -- together with Semsudin Halebic's security officer of the Jablanica staff, I interviewed Alija Turkic? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, that is the passage I mean. I've already asked you about the situation with taking a statement from Ivan Pranjic. And can I ask you whether the same comments that you made about the Pranjic statement would apply to a taking of a statement from Alija Turkic? In other words, would you expect that these interviewing officers, Salihamidzic and Halebic - I appreciate you don't know them personally - but would you expect them to have taken a proper statement from those -- from Alija Turkic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely. Plus we see Mr. Salihamidzic here reinforced by a security officer from Jablanica. So you have two qualified persons on the spot interviewing Mr. Alija Turkic. I think it would have been more than useful, even compulsory, for them to take a written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And would you mind just explaining very quickly to the Court -- you see there's a reference there to the Jablanica OPS. What is the OPS? Is that a military security body or is it a body of the State Security Services?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a municipal staff. In September 1993, there appear to still have been Municipal Staffs around. Before that, we used to have Municipal Defence Staffs. However, when on the 15th of April the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were established -- well, there's something that strikes me as weird about this military command or staff existing, so in that sense I have certain reservations but there certainly does call to mind the position of security officer of the Municipal Staff, probably with organisational duties. But it's not specified here which Municipal Staff. The army's Municipal Staff? The Territorial Defence Municipal Staff? Or from an altogether different area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Well, -- all right. Well, yes. Thank you for that. The final matter I want to ask you about from this particular document is to be found at the -- probably the second-last major paragraph. I think it would be on page 5 of the English version. And it's the -- it -- just excuse me. I'll just find you the proper place. It's a section commencing with the words: "At around 2030 hours on the 10th of September, 1993, I was informed by Sead Brankovic, a Mostar SDB State Security Service employee" -- it's on the final page of this document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you have that section?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, from reading this document in the past, you're aware of the involvement of a man from Mostar SDB named Sead Brankovic; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from this that he was included, but I know that there was a detachment. It's an organ of the Mostar centre security service -- of the State Security Service in Konjic, and you can see from this that Mr. Brankovic is a member of that service, of that detachment, or perhaps directly from the Mostar State Security Service. I cannot state definitely that he was from the Konjic detachment, but it says that he was from the Mostar State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it's apparent from the document that there was reference -- I'm going to ask you a question about what this -- what this meant to you when you read it, but it's apparent from reading this document there that Brankovic, Salihamidzic, and Namik Dzankovic went to Zulfikar Alispago's flat and then after that had a meeting when Ramiz Delalic, Celo, appeared. And I want to ask you a question about this. You see the account that these people give about Ramiz Delalic's behaviour? And if you -- if you need to, just read it to yourself and refresh your recollection about what they were saying about Ramiz Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the text, and I've read it. I have this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. You gave some evidence yesterday about encounters that you had with Ramiz Delalic and the way in which Ramiz Delalic appeared to regard the system of command and control. And my question to you is: Does this behaviour of Delalic's, as it's described here, appear consistent with what you knew of -- of Ramiz Delalic, from your own experience?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. I'm speaking this out of a certain feeling. It resembles the way that he would react, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You see there that it's attributed to Ramiz Delalic, Celo, that he appears to be if not blaming, then involving Vehbija Karic in the events? Do you see that passage there, where he mentions the name Vehbija Karic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you know Vehbija Karic personally?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was he a colonel in the JNA before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was he married to a woman of Croatian origin and did he have a -- a son with her, who was half Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did. But this is a private matter, so I didn't really dwell on that. But I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I just want to indicate that I'm not going to ask you to comment on private matters other than that bare fact. But I do have a further question: To your knowledge, Vehbija Karic was a responsible and even-tempered and professional military officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And even though you were far away in Sarajevo and you were not on the ground in Herzegovina, you yourself didn't believe for one minute that Karic would be capable of saying any such stupid thing as is described there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this line of questioning as to what the witness feels Karic would or would not have done. It's not an appropriate line of questioning to this particular witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, I believe that you have to establish some foundations for asking this question, whether this witness has some relevance, you know, to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I -- I can deal with the matter in a -- in a different way. I'll ask -- I'll ask the question in a different form or ask a different form of question, and that may be appropriate in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you regard it, knowing -- knowing Karic as you did know him, would you regard it as in character or out of character for Karic to say such a thing as is attributed to him here?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would still object. It -- the characterisation has not changed. This question is exactly the same as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's -- I've got a dispute that it's exactly the same. But I can indicate that it's always open in an appropriate case to ask a witness to evaluate the realities of a particular situation. This case from the Prosecution's side involves an -- I withdraw any speech that's about to follow. But I -- I'd submit it's relevant because Mr. Karic, Your Honour -- I understand the Prosecution have taken a deposition from him, which you asked Mr. Re about two weeks ago, and no doubt that will be before the Court in due course. But, of course, there are allegations being made about Mr. Karic of a very grave kind in this Court, and it's perfectly appropriate that Your Honours be given a proper picture of how Mr. Karic normally behaved, because the Defence case about that, you'll recall is twofold. I really have to deal with this matter as a matter of relevance to the Defence case. We say, first of all, that Mr. Halilovic wasn't present at any alleged meeting when Mr. Karic is supposed to have done this. So we can't have direct instructions on the matter, of course, because what he's saying is, well, he wasn't present. But even so, we do not concede at any time and we're not going to concede that Mr. Karic said anything like that, and in fact we put to those witnesses that the thing is an invention stemming from Musa Hota and -- and going through another chain of reporting, as one might characterise it. So that's the Defence case. And we are entitled in doing that to lead evidence about Mr. Karic. We're entitled to do that. We have to do it. I have to do it through a witness who knows him. Now, Mr. Jasarevic has given the evidence that he knows him. He's plainly entitled to comment. I'm not allowed to ask him whether it happened or not, but I am allowed to ask him whether it's in character or not. And that's why I ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You know, the problem lies in character or out of character, you know. It's very difficult, I believe, for anybody to answer this question, you know. Maybe you could use some, you know, very plain language, you know, to come across your ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll -- I'll put it -- I'll put the same question in a plainer form so that there's no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Counsel. I have brought this matter up before, and it's happened again. The objections and the speeches counsel makes in front of a witness, giving their entire Defence theory, and the witness is listening as to what their -- what their view is on the matter, what they're alleging, whether anybody said certain things or not, while the witness sits there, Your Honour, I think it's most inappropriate. It will be tantamount to the Prosecution telling Your Honours what the Prosecution theory is while the witness is sitting there and is a Prosecution witness. And I think -- I think it's quite within counsel's right to -- to sort of say to the Bench --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- what his view on the matter is. But these long speeches, giving away a lot of the intended answers, is inappropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But sometimes the Defence counsel has to put their case before this witness, including their theory and their attitude towards a certain matter, and the witness is your witness. He could agree or he has the full right to disagree with the Defence. Of course in the future proceedings it would be better not to discuss any matters which is not directly related to the particular witness in front of him. But that particular question is allowed. The problem is that we are not quite satisfied with the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can deal with the matter in a yet third way, and I'll try to do better, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, had you ever known in the past Mr. Karic to say anything as criminally irresponsible and stupid as the words that are attributed to him here in this report?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've known Mr. Karic from before the war. I knew him during the war. I know him as a very moral and serious person. I was not out in the field and I don't know whether he said that or not, but I would never assume that such a person could say anything as remotely as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. In all your dealings with Vehbija Karic, you had seen him to be a thoroughly professional and sensible officer who shared the goals of the Bosnian army; namely, a multi-ethnic Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I offer that document, MFI222, for tender, appreciating that it's -- that Mr. Salihamidzic himself is coming. Nevertheless, it was an annex to the Dzankovic document, which is already in evidence, at least in the copy that went to this witness. And so I offer it for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I want to show you another document now, Mr. Jasarevic, and this is the -- it's in the same document, as a matter of fact, as the one that's open now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's page 1 of the English document. But the B/C/S version is page 3 of the B/C/S document that's been the -- the witness currently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to show -- give the witness -- because there's more of these highlighter markings that make it hard to read the -- read the B/C/S, I want to show the witness a copy -- a paper copy. Could I just indicate that on this there are some markings by our investigators that are recent markings, and I'll hold it up so that you can see. They are brown -- brown texter markings on there. Those are additions later by the Defence team when they discovered this document and looked at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that you have to show it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's -- it is that document which is scanned, and that should be in the -- I'm very happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, especially, you know, the marks by your investigations. They are entitled to look at it to see whether there's any tricks on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course, Your Honour. I just indicate that those very marks are in fact on the B/C/S version that's on the computer, but Your Honour is right and of course we don't have any difficulty with that being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If you'd just take that moment to look at that document, please. This may or may not be a document that you've seen before, and I'm going to ask you that question in a moment, whether you've seen it before. But if you'd just look over it and see whether or not this is part of the documentation that is -- that passed through your hands at some stage in the time following Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document before, and I don't recall whether it was part of the Trebevic operation set of documents for the use of the teams. I cannot remember seeing this document before. I think I'm seeing it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I don't think we have that document. I still have the last document on the screen. I can't see this new document. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is this the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What's the number for that? Would you please repeat it. Is it D149?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: D -- sorry, the -- in terms of MFI numbers, it's -- it's to be MFI223. The number on the top of it -- of the one which I'm showing the witness now is D149(a) -- oh, sorry. Pardon me. It's not D149(a). It's D149. And it's -- commences with the words: "Croats used to live in the suburbs of Grabovica." And it has -- on the right-hand side, to distinguish it from -- it's very similar to the other document. It's very similar to it. But you'll see on the right-hand side an address, SDB, Mostar Sector, to Alica Bilic personally, SDB Konjic branch office to Nedzad Surkovic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just ask you a couple of questions about these people.. Do you know who Alica Bilic was? Or is still.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him personally. During the war, there were periods when we were in contact with each other. This man was an officer of the State Security Service in the Mostar sector. He was a prominent person. He was the man in charge of the intelligence centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, because this didn't pass through your hands, I'm just going to limit my questions about it because it will be appropriate to lead it through another witness. But I just ask you to indicate: This is a State Security document and passes apparently through the line of state security from the Mostar state security person in Jablanica to Alica Bilic in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see who it's addressed to and a copy goes to the Konjic detachment, to Mr. Surkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And although you don't have a specific memory of this document yourself, it is the type of document which should have been included in the Trebevic investigations along with thousands of others, no doubt, at a later time when -- when Trebevic came to be executed; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Because we compiled everything that we could up there. There's no need for me to repeat that. It will probably -- the term -- its time will come. But I don't recall the document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. And I accept your evidence about that. But it appears to you anyway to be consistent with the -- with -- being consistent with coming from that person in the other report, Sead Brankovic, who was referred to in the Salihamidzic report that you just looked at; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the reporting system along the vertical line in the Internal Affairs organ. So that an indication of that reporting method.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I offer that document for tender, and we'll deal with it -- if there's an objection to it, we'll deal with it at a later time, when we deal with all of these documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, now herein lies my problem in this: This is a document. We've been shown a couple of pages on the screen. I don't know how many pages it is. I don't know what else is in this document. We have not been given this document. And I would have no way of finding out before my re-examination if there's anything else in this document I ought to know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I can assist with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- well, since this document has already been used by the Defence and is already in the system, in the e-court system, and the -- I believe that the Prosecution have the access to this document from now on. And if not, Mr. Morrissey, would you please be kind enough to furnish a copy to Madam Chana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will do that. And there may be an easier way for them to achieve that outcome, because Brankovic was a witness of theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. And -- but anyway, we'll deal with the admission of the document at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. Okay. Now, what remains for -- for questioning now are really two matters. I have to take you back to some of the rules effectively for brief expert comment, and I will do that. After that, I'm going to take you through certain documents that relate to the -- the information that went to and fro within your organisation in September of 1993. My questions are -- will take us up to the time when Mr. Sefer Halilovic was questioned during Trebevic, and that will be effectively the end of the questions, so that's -- that's what's coming: A section on the rules and then a section on some of the correspondence which I'll -- which I'll take you to. Now, would you just excuse me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well -- sorry. Just excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I'm now going to ask you some questions about the criminal procedure generally. I'll take you to some provisions. I bear in mind that you've answered my learned friend's questions already, so that I won't traverse every step of the way with those. But firstly, the crime of murder was illegal in the state of Bosnia because of the Criminal Procedure Code which, among other things, forbids that particular crime; is that correct? Is that where we find the -- the law against murder?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It's a crime of the utmost seriousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You'll have to forgive me for asking these -- these questions that obviously you take for granted in some respects, but I have to build this up step by step so that the Tribunal knows and -- knows how -- how these crimes were dealt with. Murder being a crime under the Criminal Code, the Criminal Code also provided --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Or perhaps could the witness please be shown Exhibit D136, which is already in evidence now. This is extracts of certain parts of Criminal Code. While that's being brought up on the screen, Mr. Jasarevic, I'm going to show you sections 148 and 151, but particularly 148.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And while that's being brought up, I'll explain why I'm asking you. It was the duty of all citizens to denounce grave crimes such as murder pursuant to Article 148 of the Criminal Code. Is that your understanding of the -- of the situation?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're just awaiting that. I understand sometimes these things take a time to bring up. That's -- that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt counsel. Before we carry on, I would like to see this section 148 because the witness is not a lawyer, and I don't know whether he's been asked for his professional opinion as a military security officer or as a legal consultant in respect of the Criminal Code, and it's not up on the screen. So if counsel would wait so we can see it and we can see what it actually says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we'll wait. But I think the question asked by Defence counsel is a question belonging to the common knowledge. But anyway, we'll wait for that specific article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: While we are waiting now for that, I might ask you this question,

utterances.speaker: MR. JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Because of your work and because of your experience, you are familiar with that provision without having to be shown it; is that correct? Of course we are going to show it to you as well, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that these are principles, and in this area you couldn't live without these main guidelines and being acquainted with such regulations and laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I indicate what's going to occur this afternoon, just so that -- it may assist things to go as smoothly as possible. I have in mind to ask Mr. Jasarevic to comment on a -- a couple of documents. First of all, the -- the two provisions of the Criminal Code, which I wanted to show him. After that, I wanted to show him the Law on District Military Courts to indicate how it was that the civil -- the crime of murder came to be tried and was able to be tried by -- by district military courts, and that's a matter which is of importance because it shows how things were supposed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, on the screen now do you see the front page of the -- it's called Zbornik -- is that the front page of the Criminal Code, rather than my trying to pronounce it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be moved forward now to article -- it's the next page, Article 148 of that code, which is photocopied on the following page. Thank you. I'm very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you see Article 148 and also Article 149 on that page?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And is --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see 148, and I see 149 should be the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think Your Honours may recall that I slipped into this error on the previous occasion that I asked witnesses about this document that I -- I made the 148 error.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is it the duty of all citizens under both 148 but also under 149(a) -- sorry, 149(1), is it the duty of all citizens to report crimes? And in particular I'm looking now at 149(1).

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 149 article (1) you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now, having inspected those -- those provisions, but in particular 149(1), that's the fact, isn't it, citizens should report crimes when they see them as a social duty? Is that the fact?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown the following page, and in particular Article 151.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you Article 151 now, sorry, Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Does that article oblige Internal Affairs organs to take steps? I'm looking now at paragraph 1 -- to take a variety of steps in the investigation of a serious crime or a crime prosecuted ex officio?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, this was a -- a civil code -- sorry, a civilian code applicable across the board to all civilians, whether they were soldiers or -- or not. But now I want to show you another document concerning the -- the way in which military courts got their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness now please be shown -- it's D1 -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me. I'll give you the proper DD number. It is DD00.0874, and it's to be MFI224.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was the registry's understanding that it would be MFI223.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, we accept that. Your Honours, I readjust that on advice to MFI223.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I'm about to show you now when it comes up is Article 6 of the district military court's law, which appears to give jurisdiction to the -- those courts to try serious offences. Very well. Now, do you have in front of you the front page of the law on military courts?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You have Article 6. Excellent. That's the one I want you to have. Very well. Now, is it your understanding that Article 6 gave jurisdiction to the district military court to try cases involving criminal offences committed by military personnel?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we understand each other. You have Article 7 here with amendments and reference to military institutions. This may be an error. Perhaps it's just that I'm misunderstanding something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak up or speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, two matters in response to what you raised there, Mr. Jasarevic. You may detect from time to time a translation issue that we haven't seen, and you can always point that out to us. Secondly, the interpreter asks that you speak a little closer to the microphone, if that's possible. Finally, can I just ask: Do you have in front of you Article 6 or do you have Article 7?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Returning to my question, then: Is that -- is it under Article 6 that the jurisdiction of the military courts arises, in your understanding, to try serious criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. No, I'm instructed now that what you have in front of you may not be the correct page. In the Bosnian version could the witness be shown the following page after that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have that now, the relevant Article 6? Yes, I'm sorry. I was certainly -- it was my fault there, and I apologise for that. Now, do you have that jurisdictional section, Article 6?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And is that your understanding, that it's pursuant to that Article that the courts get their jurisdiction -- the military courts get their jurisdiction to try serious criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am able to interpret this, that seems to be the case. I have no other opinion to offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer that for tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you some questions about the relevant law applicable to investigations and how that's -- how that's to be dealt with. First of all, you were asked questions by the learned Prosecutor concerning military -- the Rules of Military Discipline, and I want to ask you some questions about that. Firstly, the Rules of Military Discipline to your understanding are a -- a tool that military commanders have to deal with infractions of military discipline involving the infliction of minor summary punishments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say so yesterday. Any infractions of military discipline would be under the jurisdiction of all the different bodies within the military organisation, including, of course, the security bodies. However, when these infractions grow out of volume in a manner of speaking and spill over into an area where there are potential indications of a crime, then security bodies get involved -- or rather, the military police, and professionals come in who take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And when dealing with a series of tragic and horrible murders, you don't proceed against -- you don't proceed in investigating those murders under the military discipline rules; you proceed under the SVB's rules. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can investigate under the Rules of Military Discipline and under the criminal -- instructions from criminal law, but not under the SVB rules. Or in order to make myself clear, Article 40 of the Rules of Service was virtually copied from the first section of Article 51, of the law that we saw just a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll be going to Article 40 of the SVB rules in about five minutes, but at this stage now it's -- you indicated that there were some difficulties with the -- perhaps the realism of some of Mr. Dzankovic's proposals, but it would have been an extraordinary situation for him to propose confining the men to barracks for three days or demoting them or imposing some other of the military disciplinary regimes. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I don't understand this approach or I just don't support this approach. Mr. Dzankovic as a member of the inspection team in this case had no competence, no power, and no authority, because after all he had never received an order from the commander that he could then see through. It would have been very difficult for him to find himself in a situation like that. I did try to explain a while ago about these circumstances, so I don't think I should waste any more time now, unless counsel insists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, I don't insist. I'm properly chastised. I'm sorry. Sometimes my comprehension --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, look, can I ask now that the witness be shown the document which was tendered already, the SVB rules. It's D13 -- yes, the Defence document D137. That's not a 65 ter number. That's an exhibit number. That's already been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, could we have a break now, and during the break I hope you could approach the court deputy about the documents you are going to use --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- in the next session so we could save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we'll resume at quarter past 4.00, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey. I saw the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. Do you see before you on -- on the screen now the front page of the SVB rules?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could the SVB rules now please be turned to Articles 40 and 41. I think they are both on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. We're just awaiting the English version. Okay. Thank you. Do you have Article 40 in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, that article appears to provide an obligation for the military security service to take necessary measures to find the perpetrator of the criminal offence, to prevent the perpetrator and his accomplices from going into hiding or escaping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just ask that the next page in the English be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: "To uncover and protect the evidence and exhibits which can be served as evidence and to gather all the information useful for successful conduct of the criminal proceedings." Now, I'm just going to ask for a couple of comments upon that passage before I go any further. First of all, does that section there deal with a part of the criminal proceeding or does it really deal with something before the criminal proceeding itself begins; in other words, the pre-criminal proceeding? Are you able to comment on that question?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a pre-criminal action. When there is reasonable suspicion, then the service must take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could I -- I'll put a proposition to you and you tell me if you agree or not. But I'll read it to you. And when I've finished, you tell me if this is right. "The activity of the SVB" -- and I'm referring here to the activity under that section. "The activity of the SVB does not represent the criminal procedure itself, but that activity is a necessary assumption which enables the initiation and effectiveness of the procedure in the first place. The matters dealt with by the services are to be relayed to the authorised military prosecutor through a criminal denunciation or an official report." Now, does that proposition I've just put to you accurately reflect what should happen during the pre-criminal phase?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there may be more flexible interpretation of the last bit. In relation to relaying this to the authorised military prosecutor, this can be quite simple, but it depends on the situation on the amount of material that has been gathered because pursuant to the Law on Military Prosecutors, as soon as a military prosecutor finds out that there are indications that a crime has been committed, he must request additional information. But I think I can accept yes as an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps to -- just to develop that a little bit. The time at which the investigating service must go to the military prosecutor really depends upon the nature of the concrete case at hand. Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, but it may depend on the circumstances, physical circumstances. Is this possible or is there still a hindrance or an obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Upon reaching a certain stage of -- well, I withdraw that. Now, the -- the competence of the -- of the services, and in particular of the SVB, to engage in that sort of investigative procedure is founded upon that section; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Could I take you now to Article number -- Article 41. And does Article 41 indicate the obligation of the military security service to submit a criminal report to the competent military prosecutor's office? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I've lost the image there. Yes, this is the first part of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the article, based on such information as has been gathered, the military security service at brigade level shall file a criminal complaint, which is in relation to what we discussed about Article 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. I just have some questions for you now about how this operated at the battalion, the brigade, and the corps level and the obligations that arose at those particular levels. Let's deal with the battalion level. If there were -- a reasonable suspicion arose under Article 40 that a -- a crime may have been committed by a particular individual, whose obligation -- sorry, at what level did -- was the SVB required to deal with that? Was it the obligation -- well, first of all, was it your obligation to be advised about and to deal with crimes at the battalion level, or was it really a matter that should be dealt with in the first instance at the battalion level?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question, the second part of your question refers to me personally, or rather, to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of explaining the different levels of deployment of the security administration, the fourth and lowest level is the battalion level. That is the least evolved level of the military security service. Intelligence and counter-intelligence are merged at that level. In terms of manpower and in terms of the number of executors, this is the weakest level. It would usually be an assistant commander. In strong battalions or independent battalions, the assistant commander would have two or three as a maximum assistant officers. But since they had an intelligence function too, he would not have been bound, as you can tell by looking at Article 1 of the Rules of Service, to file a criminal complaint but he's still under obligation to gather information and then submit the information to the brigade's security. At this point, the brigade's security service comes in and that part of the job is done at this particular level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And at the brigade level -- where -- where the security service at the brigade level finds itself involved in an investigation, who bears the -- the obligation of contacting the -- of making a criminal report at that point? Should the brigade level operative do it or do they need to come to you for permission about that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no need to see me about permission. There would have been no need to go to the corps for permission in that matter -- for that matter. The brigade has its own military police. What you have to look at is that this unit has its own military police attached. This unit has both authority and certain competencies as part of the criminal proceeding. It is an institution which has the use of force as an option available. If you go by the principles, this could have ended right at the brigade level. If they were dealing with a more complex case, in that case they would have gone to the assistant commander of the corps. What was especially important in wartime conditions was our cooperation with the different bodies of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. I just want to turn to the -- the issue of where an -- where a security service officer finds himself being blocked by his commander. Now, let's take the example of a -- of a brigade -- of a situation at brigade level where an SVB operative is performing his proper investigative duties but he finds that the brigade commander is obstructing his work. Is it the SVB operative's obligation in that situation to report up the professional line to the next level, to the corps?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I spoke about the authority of the military security service. I spoke about all the functions, and in principle this worked up the line through the three different levels, across the three levels. When speaking about the second and third functions, I pointed out then and I do now that there is a very significant element, especially in wartime conditions. It would have been highly impractical - and I happen to believe also impracticable - under combat conditions, or if combat was about to begin, or just after combat they would have been facing a whole range of difficulties. The military security service or the military police would not have been in a position to commence -- to take any pre-investigation steps. The best solution would have been for the commander to -- to issue an order. This is due to the very nature of military organisation. This is an important matter and a matter like this could not have been done without the brigade commander issuing the relevant orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Now, in that situation, just in the situation of -- of a blocking or a failure by the brigade commander to -- to do their job, not merely of inactivity but a positive interference, for example, with the investigation - I'm remaining in the hypothetical situation that we're in - in that situation, the brigade SVB officer should report up the line, shouldn't they? Up the professional line, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand you fully, and this is definitely the case. You have an example from the 9th Brigade to that effect. There were certain cases of obstruction, if you like, or blockade, or maybe the military security service was not sufficiently free to go about their work. The security service of the 9th Brigade informed the corps, and this is precisely how we know about certain information, and we have more information than in relation to the 10th Brigade, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and you indicated that's because Tomo Juric was a sensible functioning security officer doing his job.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. Well, in the concrete case that's before the Court now, you did not receive from Namik Dzankovic any complaint that he was being blocked by Sefer Halilovic. Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. What I propose to do now is to take you through a number of documents. There's -- there may be 20, as a matter of fact. These documents, broadly speaking, are directions, letters, communications of various sorts that passed in the -- in the SVB service in the days and weeks after the killings at Grabovica. Now, I'll make it clear that some of these documents are old documents and some of them you may have seen before. Some of them you certainly will not have seen. With respect to those that you haven't seen, I'm going to ask you for an expert type of comment, and you can advise us what the situation is, in terms of whether you've seen them or not, and feel free to comment as you feel inclined to do with these ones because, frankly, you were there and we weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown, first of all,- just excuse me a moment - the exhibit which has already been tendered, D153.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The document I'm about to show you, while it's being brought up on the screen -- the document I'm about to show you is one you may well not have seen, but I'm going to ask you for a professional comment about it. It's a document which has been tendered in evidence already and is a communication between officers of the 44th Brigade, which was a local Jablanica brigade, and the 6th Corps with certain information in it.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. Very well. I would ask you then just to offer a professional comment upon it. Thank you. First of all, can you comment on the -- just can you confirm a couple of details. Do you see that it's addressed from the 44th Mountain Brigade to the 6th Corps command military security sector in Konjic and dated the 9th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And does it appear to you -- I understand you haven't seen the document before, but does the information appear to you to be typically operative information which is being passed along to the 6th Corps military security sector concerning the possibility of some killings at Grabovica in the night between the 8th and 9th of September and the arrival of 250 refugees on the same night in Jablanica from the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this line of questioning. It's the very same what we the Prosecution did. We would show the witness a document, he says he has never seen it before, and yet this time the witness has been asked to comment on information within that and whether it's operative information or not. I'm not sure what the witness is being asked about in respect of a document he's not seen. It's not his document. He's never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that depends on the contents of this document, whether the witness is familiar with what is written there or not. But we'll test how far the witness will go concerning of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But I think I should deal with a couple of matters raised there, because it could be important in the way that other documents are used too. So -- I just indicate this: First of all, this document is already in evidence, and what I'm asking for is an expert comment by a person who's the head of this particular service as to -- first of all I'm going to ask about structurally speaking how should, according to the rules, the 6th Corps have responded to this -- to this material. I'm not asking him to confirm whether it's true or not, because of course he doesn't know that. I wouldn't ask him that question. But it's -- he's obviously clearly able to comment on, given the rules of the SVB, what should have happened when this document arrived at the 6th Corps, and that's really what I want to ask him, what -- what nature of report would he expect and should occur within his service. Now, that's plainly admissible. It's -- it's relevant, so I'd seek to proceed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now, having regard to that document, Mr. Jasarevic, I'm not asking you to confirm or deny the truth of the contents of it, because I understand you weren't down in Jablanica at that time and didn't see it. But what I'm asking you about is what action should the 6th Corps, which received -- the 6th Corps security services have taken upon receiving this document? What should they have done in the normal course of events, according to your rules?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military security service, having received such a document from a subordinate from some brigade, would receive it, study it, analyse it, and assess what was the important thing in such a document. Since this document indicates that there were murders, this would then lead to the conclusion that there was a crime. In view of the gravity of such an act, it would be important to inform the superior or the -- the corps security service about this. Along with such information being passed on to them, the commander of the corps would also be informed about it, because these are serious questions, and the security service in its way is a command service, so it is something that it would have to inform about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you for that. And I'll ask you one question -- you may not have any personal knowledge of this matter, and if you don't, you don't. Do you know whether -- do you from your own knowledge know whether or not any statements -- well, look, I withdraw that question. I'll deal with that issue a bit later on. Very well. Thank you. Now, I want to take you to another document. You said - and I'll just put a couple of preliminary questions first - do you recall giving evidence - I think it was when my learned friend asked you questions - concerning the first news that you heard about the killings in Grabovica. And I think you indicated that you received a phone call, and it may have been on approximately the 11th of -- of September, and you weren't at that -- and now 11 years later you weren't able to recall who gave you that phone call. Now, this document may be -- may be relevant, may be able to assist you. I'm not sure. I just want to give you the chance to look at and it you make any comment you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But could the witness please be shown now -- its 65 ter number is D26. Its ERN number -- or its eight-digit number is DD00.2575, and it's to be MFI224.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, this document has the appearance of a short inquiry. It may assist your memory. But just take the opportunity to look at and it then I'll ask you some questions about it. Could I just ask you a question first of all: Do you notice in the first line of this document here, there's a reference to "unverified information." And I just wanted to ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry, counsel. I do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Neither do I. But it's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It may have appeared just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Jasarevic. We have technical hitches from time to time. There's a reference in this document here you'll see to "unverified information." It's in the first line of the text there. Could I ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Are you able to comment? Is that -- is that a reference -- that term "unverified information," is that a reference to the phone call that you mentioned in evidence that -- that you received telling you that something had happened on the 11th of -- of September?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably by telephone. Perhaps also through unofficial direct contacts outside of the official premises. But most probably it was through the official telephone. What I called "unverified," I've already emphasised that it was important for me the type of information I received and from whom. So I probably then said that it was unverified, and I also indicate here that it is necessary to react quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I won't ask you questions about that again, because you were very clear on the topic of -- of the sort of -- of the way you dealt with operative information. Could I just have -- I just need some formal questions effectively to be answered about this document here. First of all, this document -- can I ask you this: How long is it since you saw a copy of this document? Is it many years, or have you been shown it in recent times?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the investigators of this Tribunal showed it to me when I was giving my statement, but also when I was given a series of documents that I was supposed to identify. I think that that's when it was, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So as far as you know, anyway, this document was in the Prosecution's hands because they showed it to you at one stage; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I probably was shown it by the investigators during the identification of the documents. There were many documents from the Prosecution. It's possible that this one was also amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, now, just dealing with it -- with some specifics about it. This document is dated "Sarajevo, 12th of September, 1993." Is there any indication on the document about the time when it was written? I notice there's a time down at the bottom next to -- or near to the name "Arnautovic," but that seems to relate to something else. Is there a time on -- when this document was composed on this -- anywhere on this letter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you can see down here, that's written by hand: "The communications centre, Supreme Command Staff, signed by Arnautovic. This is the communications centre at the staff which received and decoded the messages. You can see that this was received on the 13th, and the time is 1528 hours, and you can see that the document was drafted on the 12th. Probably it was written on the 11th in the evening. I conclude this not by my memory but by my initials in the lower right-hand corner, because I didn't give it to any of my subordinates in the administration to type it out. I very rarely myself actually typed a document, so I assume that this was in the evening when people were already resting and because of the speed required to respond to this, I most probably typed this myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. That's your signature; is that correct? Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and the "JJ" -- what you just referred to a moment ago, the "JJ," is that "JJ" on the left-hand side of the page towards the bottom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are my initials. This is what I spoke about. Then "/JZ." That is the typist, the operator who did that. It's a woman. Her name is Jasna Zametica; she's an employee at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, that resolves that -- that matter. The person to whom it is addressed is not named, but by chief of the military service of the 6th Corps, you understood that to be Nermin Eminovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And so, in summary, this document here was a document which was an urgent document done in response to some very disturbing news which you had heard on the telephone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF JASAREVIC [Resumed]
